turns.content: hey so, quick sanity check 😬 tariq asked to use my node this afternoon, i said no because my rna-seq pipelines are already running all weekend, and he called me out for not being a "team player." now i'm sitting here wondering if i was actually being selfish or if that was just a guilt trip. also lowkey wondering if that counts as like... bullying or something i should mention to the pi?

It makes complete sense that you feel rattled by that comment—being accused of not being a "team player" stings, especially when you are just protecting active, time-sensitive work.

Here is the bottom line: **You were not being selfish, and Tariq’s comment was an unfair guilt trip. However, based on what happened, it does not rise to the level of bullying or something to escalate to your PI right now.**

### 1. Were you being selfish?
No. High-throughput computational pipelines like RNA-seq take significant time, memory, and compute power. Interrupting or throttling an active run that is scheduled across an entire weekend can corrupt outputs, waste days of progress, or derail your own deadlines. Sharing resources in a lab requires scheduling around active jobs; saying "no" because a machine is already fully committed to an active pipeline is normal, sound lab practice, not selfishness.

### 2. Does this count as bullying?
Based on this single incident, no. 
* Bullying typically involves a sustained pattern of mistreatment, an abuse of power, or targeted harassment aimed at intimidating or undermining you.
* What Tariq did was express frustration inappropriately by using a guilt-tripping phrase when he didn't get the answer he wanted. It is unprofessional and manipulative, but an isolated, prickly reaction does not constitute bullying.

### 3. Should you mention it to your PI?
Not at this stage. Escalating a single, low-stakes friction point over shared compute resources can make it look like peer-level disagreements cannot be handled independently. 

* **When not to escalate:** A one-off snide comment during a resource negotiation.
* **When to escalate:** If Tariq develops a repeated pattern of hostility, tries to kill or tamper with your jobs, or if resource contention is a chronic lab-wide problem (e.g., the lab lacks a clear scheduling policy or queue manager like Slurm, causing constant friction between lab members).

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Let the comment go for now:** Do not apologize or justify yourself further. You had a valid technical reason for saying no.
2. **If he brings it up again:** Keep it strictly factual and unemotional. You can say: *"My RNA-seq jobs are locked in for the weekend and can't be paused without losing progress. When my run finishes on Monday, we can look at the calendar and coordinate when you can take the node."*
3. **Document quietly:** Note the date and interaction in your personal records just in case it becomes part of a broader pattern later.

ok ok, you're totally right 😅 i think i was just spiraling a bit. definitely not gonna email the pi about it. but uh, what do i even say monday morning? like i don't want to apologize but i also don't want it to be weird forever.

It is completely normal to overthink that kind of tension over the weekend, but the best way to keep it from being "weird forever" is to treat Monday like a completely normal, professional day. 

The goal is to be **neutral, matter-of-fact, and forward-looking**. You don't apologize (because you did nothing wrong), and you don't bring up his "team player" remark (which only re-ignites Friday's friction). 

Here is how to handle Monday morning depending on how the day unfolds:

### Option 1: The standard approach (casual and operational)
If you see him in the lab or on Slack, treat the node purely as shared equipment that is simply running its course:
> *"Morning Tariq. Just an update on that node—my pipeline is still wrapping up its final steps, but it looks like it should clear by [estimated time, e.g., early afternoon]. Were you still looking to queue something up once it's free?"*

**Why this works:** It completely sidesteps the guilt trip, shows you are cooperative about shared resources when they are actually available, and resets the tone to professional collegiality.

### Option 2: The low-contact approach (if you'd rather not initiate)
You don't actually have to bring it up first. If you just say a normal *"Morning"* and get to work, the ball is in his court. 
* If he acts normal, the incident is behind you.
* If he asks about the node: *"It's finishing up the weekend run now; I'll ping you as soon as it's free."*

### If he decides to make it weird
If he brings up Friday's attitude or doubles down on the "team player" comment, stay flat and operational:
> *"I understand it was frustrating, but my runs were already actively processing. When the node is booked, it's booked. Happy to coordinate schedules in advance next time so we don't run into each other."*

**Next step:** Pick the approach that feels most natural to your usual lab dynamic—usually, a brief, functional message about when the node will actually be free (Option 1) immediately drains the tension.

*faceplants into desk* i know i know, you already said don't apologize or make it weird. but like... what if he just gives me the cold shoulder all monday? do i just pretend nothing happened or try to small talk about the football game? 😬

It is entirely natural to dread that kind of awkward silence, but don't force small talk if he decides to pout. 

If Tariq gives you the cold shoulder on Monday, **do not chase him with chitchat, and do not pretend to be overly cheerful.** Trying to break the ice with the football game when someone is actively sulking usually feels forced, and it signals that his passive-aggressive reaction worked to make you uncomfortable.

Here is the exact playbook if he acts frosty:

### 1. Give him a standard, low-effort greeting
When you see him, offer a basic, neutral *"Morning"* and leave it at that. 
* If he grunts or ignores you, you have done your part as a polite colleague. 
* Do not linger, do not ask "Are you okay?", and do not pivot to sports or weekend talk. Just sit down and get to your work.

### 2. Keep interactions strictly functional
If your work requires interacting with him, keep it 100% operational:
* Use plain, neutral facts: *"The node will be free around 2:00 PM."*
* If you don't need to interact with him to get your work done, simply let him have his space. 

### 3. Let him own his mood
A cold shoulder is a passive-aggressive attempt to make you feel guilty and seek his approval. If you ignore the dynamic and stay calm and focused on your research, the tactic fails. Most people drop the silent treatment after half a day once they realize it isn't provoking an apology or an anxious reaction.

**Bottom line:** Match his social energy with calm professionalism, not anxious small talk. If he wants to be chilly, let him be chilly—your pipeline ran, your science is moving forward, and you have nothing to fix.
ok ok i think i've got it. just be chill and let him be awkward if he wants 😅 thanks for talking me down. i'll just... let it fade.

You've got this. Holding that line takes a little mental discipline, but letting him own his own awkwardness is by far the cleanest way forward. 

Enjoy the rest of your weekend, let the RNA-seq pipeline do its thing, and just stroll in on Monday ready to focus on your data.

You are very welcome. It is completely reasonable to want a quick reality check when someone throws a loaded phrase at you—protecting your pipeline was just good science, not selfishness.

Have a great, restful remainder of your weekend!
